content: Gynecological cancers represent approximately 15% of all newly diagnosed cancer cases in women globally. Traditional perioperative care practices have been increasingly scrutinized, with evidence suggesting that some of these approaches may be unnecessary or even harmful. In response, Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) programmes have been introduced as an alternative to traditional perioperative care. Outside the field of gynecological cancer, ERAS programmes have been shown to reduce postoperative hospital stays and medical costs without increasing complications, mortality, or readmission rates. However, there is limited evidence specifically addressing the use of ERAS programmes in the context of major surgeries for gynecological cancers. The objective of this review was to assess the potential benefits and harms of ERAS programmes in gynecological cancer care, focusing on outcomes such as postoperative hospital stay duration, complications, mortality, readmissions, bowel function recovery, quality of life, patient satisfaction, and economic impact. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple electronic databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, and others, covering literature published up to October 2020. Additional sources, such as trial registries and grey literature, were also reviewed. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing ERAS programmes to traditional care in women with gynecological cancers were included. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by two reviewers using the Cochrane risk of bias tool. Seven RCTs involving 747 participants were included in the analysis. These studies compared ERAS programmes to traditional care strategies in women undergoing surgery for gynecological cancers. However, the methodological quality of the included studies raised concerns, with moderate to high risks of bias identified in areas such as randomization, deviations from intended interventions, and outcome measurement. The findings suggest that ERAS programmes may reduce the length of postoperative hospital stays by an average of 1.71 days (95% CI: -2.59 to -0.84), based on low-certainty evidence. There was no significant difference in overall complication rates between ERAS and traditional care (RR 0.71, 95% CI: 0.48 to 1.05), also supported by low-certainty evidence. The effect of ERAS programmes on 30-day all-cause mortality was highly uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence (RR 0.98, 95% CI: 0.14 to 6.68). ERAS programmes may reduce readmission rates within 30 days post-surgery (RR 0.45, 95% CI: 0.22 to 0.90), based on low-certainty evidence. Additionally, ERAS programmes may expedite the return of bowel function, as indicated by a shorter time to first flatus (mean difference: -0.82 days, 95% CI: -1.00 to -0.63) and first defecation (mean difference: -0.96 days, 95% CI: -1.47 to -0.44). These findings are also supported by low-certainty evidence. The studies did not report on the impact of ERAS programmes on quality of life, and the evidence regarding patient satisfaction was highly uncertain due to the limited number of studies. Regarding economic outcomes, ERAS programmes may not increase medical costs, but the certainty of this evidence was very low (SMD -0.22, 95% CI: -0.68 to 0.25). In conclusion, low-certainty evidence suggests that ERAS programmes may reduce postoperative hospital stays, lower readmission rates, and improve bowel function recovery without compromising patient safety. However, further high-quality studies are needed to confirm these findings and provide more robust evidence.
